title: Σαλπιγκτής
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 325. Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Σαλπιγκτὴς στρατὸν ἐπισυνάγων καὶ κρατηθεὶς ὑπὸ τῶν πολεμίων ἐβόα· « Μὴ κτείνετέ με, ὦ ἄνδρες, εἰκῆ καὶ μάτην· οὐδένα γὰρ ὑμῶν ἀπέκτεινα· πλὴν γὰρ τοῦ χαλκοῦ τούτου οὐδὲν ἄλλο κτῶμαι. »
sentences.tr: Salpinktēs straton episynagōn kai kratētheis hypo tōn polemiōn eboa· « Mē kteinete me, ō andres, eikē kai matēn· oudena gar hymōn apekteina· plēn gar tou chalkou toutou ouden allo ktōmai. »
sentences.l: A trumpeter, mustering an army and having been overpowered by the enemy, kept crying out: « Do not kill me, men, idly and to no purpose; for I have killed none of you; for apart from this bronze I possess nothing else. »
sentences.i: A trumpeter who was mustering an army was taken by the enemy, and cried out: « Do not kill me, men, for nothing and to no purpose. I have killed none of you — I have no property at all except this bronze. »
sentences.n: The fable's usual engine: a chain of participles (ἐπισυνάγων, κρατηθείς) carrying the action, with the one finite verb ἐβόα, an imperfect, holding the shouting open. ὁ χαλκός, 'the bronze', is his trumpet, named by the metal it is made of. εἰκῆ καὶ μάτην doubles two near-synonyms for emptiness, as Greek likes to do in a plea. κτάομαι in the present is strictly 'acquire'; the perfect κέκτημαι is 'possess', and later Greek lets the present slide into that sense, as here.

sentences.t: Οἱ δὲ πρὸς αὐτὸν ἔφασαν· « Διὰ τοῦτο γὰρ μᾶλλον τεθνήξῃ, ὅτι σὺ μὴ δυνάμενος πολεμεῖν τοὺς πάντας πρὸς μάχην ἐγείρεις. »
sentences.tr: Hoi de pros auton ephasan· « Dia touto gar mallon tethnēxēi, hoti sy mē dynamenos polemein tous pantas pros machēn egeireis. »
sentences.l: And they said to him: « For this very reason you shall die the more, because you, not being able to fight, rouse everyone to battle. »
sentences.i: And they said to him: « That is all the more reason for you to die: you cannot fight yourself, and you rouse everyone else to battle. »
sentences.n: τεθνήξῃ is a future perfect, 'you shall be dead' — the ordinary Greek future for dying, and blunter than a plain future would be. διὰ τοῦτο … ὅτι takes up the trumpeter's own defence and turns it into the charge.

sentences.t: Ὁ μῦθος δηλοῖ ὅτι πλέον πταίουσιν οἱ τοὺς κακοὺς καὶ βαρεῖς δυνάστας ἐπεγείροντες εἰς τὸ κακοποιεῖν.
sentences.tr: Ho mythos dēloi hoti pleon ptaiousin hoi tous kakous kai bareis dynastas epegeirontes eis to kakopoiein.
sentences.l: The fable shows that those who rouse up wicked and oppressive lords to the doing of harm are the more at fault.
sentences.n: πταίω is properly to stumble, and so either to come to grief or to be at fault; the trumpeter's judges have just settled which is meant here — the man who does no harm himself is the more blameable for setting others on. βαρύς of a ruler is 'heavy, hard to bear'. εἰς τὸ κακοποιεῖν is an articular infinitive with εἰς, expressing the end for which they are roused.
